items.title: The Easy, Low-Cost Ways Bengaluru Locals Keep Street Dogs Dry & Fed in the Rains
items.blurb: Every June, as the first heavy showers flood Bengaluru's low-lying wards, a familiar routine kicks in across hundreds of homes near community dog spots. Someone hunts for a cardboard box in the storeroom, wraps a tarpaulin around it, and leaves it under the compound gate before the next downpour. It looks like a small gesture. For an estimated 2,70,000 stray dogs living through the city's monsoon, it can be the difference between staying dry and developing a fever that turns dangerous within days. Bengaluru's community feeders, canine squads and shelters have spent years working out what actually helps a street dog survive the wet months, and their routine has settled into a clear chain. A dry dog needs to stay fed. A well-fed dog can still fall sick if its food or water carries bacteria. And even the healthiest dog can pick up a wound or a tick that, left untreated, becomes an emergency. Shelter, food and first aid are not three separate tasks so much as one continuous act of care, and none of it requires special training or a large budget. How a cardboard box becomes a dog’s home The classic monsoon shelter starts with a sturdy cardboard box. Cut a small entrance into one side, line the inside with a sheet of plastic or tarpaulin so the cardboard itself never touches water, and place it in a raised, sheltered spot such as under a stairwell or awning. A single shelter built this way costs under Rs 500, and for larger colonies, an old blanket or banner strung between two supports does the same job. Dry kibble, plain biscuits or boiled rice with chicken or egg can provide community dogs with nutritious food without upsetting their digestion during the rains. Locality groups such as Cubbon Park Canines, which feeds around 120 dogs in the park, and the wider network run by the CJ Memorial Trust track which dogs use which shelters, so a missing animal is noticed within a day rather than a week. Some squads go further and fit dogs with reflective collars so they stay visible after dark, when rain and poor visibility raise the risk of road accidents. A dry dog, though, is still a hungry one, and shelter alone does not keep a stray healthy through four months of rain. The right food can make all the difference in the rains That is where feeding comes in, and here the goal is less about quantity than about keeping food dry and gentle on a stray's stomach. Dry kibble or plain biscuits, stored in an airtight container, hold up far better in the humidity than left-over curry or wet bread, and boiled rice mixed with a little boiled chicken or egg, without salt or spice, fills a dog up without upsetting its digestion. From building shelters to spotting wounds and ticks early, Bengaluru’s community feeders rely on simple daily interventions to help stray dogs survive the wet season. Most feeders now skip milk altogether, since many strays are lactose intolerant, using diluted curd instead when puppies need something soft. A clean, covered water bowl matters just as much as the food in it, since stagnant puddles are a major source of leptospirosis, a bacterial infection carried in floodwater that can prove fatal within days. Even so, a dog that is dry and well fed can still turn up with a torn ear, an embedded tick or a small cut that a fly finds before anyone else does, which is why the third habit in the chain, a basic first-aid pouch, tends to matter most during the wettest weeks. A first-aid kit that helps before the vet arrives The pouch itself fits into a tote bag. A small bottle of povidone-iodine solution, sold as Betadine or Cipladine at any chemist, cleans a fresh wound without stinging as much as spirit or Dettol, both harsher on canine skin than human skin. An antiseptic powder keeps the cleaned wound dry, which matters more in the rains since damp wounds are exactly where flies lay eggs, and a dab of an ayurvedic fly-repellent ointment such as Himax over a healing cut is often what stops it turning into a maggot wound within 48 hours. A fine-toothed tick comb or blunt tweezers lets a feeder lift an attached tick close to the skin, since a bite can pass on ehrlichiosis or babesiosis within hours; the tick then goes into soapy water, never crushed between fingers. Gloves, a torch, a soft muzzle and the saved number of a nearby vet or rescue group such as Sarvoham Animal Foundation or Charlie's Animal Rescue Centre round out the kit. What stays out is anything dosed by body weight, such as antibiotics, dewormers or ivermectin, since a guessed dose on a stray of unknown weight can do real harm. Pale gums, laboured breathing, a swollen limb or a foul-smelling wound are signs to photograph, note the location of, and report to a vet or NGO helpline at once, rather than treat at home. The pouch is built to hold a dog steady for a day or two, not to replace the vet it eventually needs. None of this depends on grand infrastructure. It depends on residents who notice a soaked, shivering dog outside their gate and decide to act, in the spirit of the couple who once turned their own compound into a shelter for over 85 rescued strays . Across Bengaluru, thousands of small acts of care decide whether a street dog makes it through the monsoon. A cardboard box, a bowl of safe food and a basic first-aid kit may seem simple, but together they can mean the difference between survival and suffering for the city’s 2.7 lakh community dogs. items.title: A Forest That Sings: How Sikkim’s Bamboo & Wood Become Traditional Lepcha Instruments
items.blurb: In Sikkim, a length of bamboo can become a flute. A piece of mature wood can become a three-stringed instrument. And, once either is played, the landscape that produced it travels far beyond the hillside where the material was found. That relationship between place, material and music received formal recognition last year. On 5 November 2025, the Government of India granted Geographical Indication (GI) registration to two traditional Lepcha musical instruments, the Tungbuk and Pumtong Pulit, under the Musical Instrument category of the Geographical Indications Registry. These instruments cannot be separated from the ecology that makes them. When a forest becomes an instrument The Tungbuk is a three-stringed instrument traditionally made from softwood and parchment. It is about 36 inches long, with a diameter of 11 inches and a height of six inches, and is used to accompany music and local dance in Sikkim. The Pumtong Pulit is different. It is a four-hole bamboo flute , traditionally made from bamboo and used, among other things, to reproduce natural sounds. Both belong to Lepcha folk music and carry cultural and spiritual significance. They are played alongside songs, dances and ceremonies, placing them within a larger musical tradition that includes bamboo flutes, drums and string instruments. But look more closely at what they are made of. The Pumtong Pulit begins with bamboo. The Tungbuk begins with wood. The choice of material affects how the instrument is made and, ultimately, how it sounds. Photograph: (PIBGangtok) The Pumtong Pulit begins with bamboo. The Tungbuk begins with wood. The choice of material affects how the instrument is made and, ultimately, how it sounds. This makes the GI recognition interesting from an ecological perspective. The instruments have a geographical identity because their making is tied to a particular cultural landscape. The people who call themselves children of nature For the Lepchas, this relationship is not new. The Government of Sikkim's Tribal Research Institute describes the Lepchas as Sikkim's original indigenous inhabitants and notes the community's close relationship with nature. It records the endoethnonym Mutanchi Rong Kup Rum Kup, while official and other sources describe Mutanchi Rongkup as referring to the community's relationship with nature and the snowy peaks. That connection runs through Lepcha cultural life. Songs, festivals and rituals are closely associated with mountains, rivers, trees and plants. The Government of Sikkim notes that prayers, offerings and ceremonies are dedicated to trees, plants, mountains, nature deities and rivers. I extend my heartiest congratulations to the Lepcha community of Sikkim on the proud achievement of receiving the Geographical Indication (GI) registration for the traditional musical instruments Tungbuk and Puntong Palit. This recognition by the Government of India is a moment… pic.twitter.com/6pjl1Jd1VO — Prem Singh Tamang (Golay) (@PSTamangGolay) November 13, 2025 Music is an integral part of Lepcha culture, with different songs accompanied by folk instruments on various occasions. So when a bamboo flute is made from a plant growing in the Himalayan landscape and then used to imitate the sounds of that landscape, the relationship between nature and culture becomes tangible. The forest is not merely the setting for the tradition. It supplies part of the tradition. A GI tag with a forest question A GI tag establishes that a product has a particular geographical origin and qualities or reputation associated with that place. It also provides legal protection against unauthorised use of the geographical name. The organisation that facilitated the GI applications, Mutanchi Lom Aal Shezum (MLAS), has said it plans workshops and awareness programmes for young people. It also intends to undertake plantation drives for two bamboo species — Po (choya bash) and Poyong — used to make the Pumtong Pulit. That detail may prove to be one of the most important parts of the GI story. Because if a musical tradition depends on bamboo, sustaining the tradition eventually means sustaining the bamboo. Planting the species used for the Pumtong Pulit therefore creates a direct connection between cultural preservation and ecological continuity . The next step could be to ensure that the geography itself continues to provide what the instruments need. Over 20 species—such as Dendrocalamus hamiltonii and Arundinaria maling —thrive across Sikkim, and the Lepchas, who consider themselves the "younger brother of bamboo," deeply integrate the plant into their heritage, daily tools, and sustainable architecture. Now, in their music too. items.title: Her Home Was Washed Away in Assam Floods. Days Later, This 17-YO Won National Gold in Karate
items.blurb: The internet signal kept disappearing. The day The Better India spoke to Janmoni Konwar, she was preparing to leave for the Sports Authority of India (SAI). Seventeen years old, the young karateka climbed towards a spot where her phone could catch a network. On the other end, her coach, Susanta Das, helped coordinate the call. Then Janmoni appeared on the screen. “Tomorrow I am going to SAI, so this is a special moment for me,” she said, breaking into a smile. It was a happy moment for a teenager about to take another step in her sporting career. But Janmoni’s journey to that moment has been anything but ordinary. Just days earlier, she had stood at Delhi’s Talkatora Indoor Stadium and won a gold medal at the National Karate Championship, held from 7 to 9 August. Competing in the Ashihara category, Janmoni had travelled from a flood-hit village in Assam to the national stage and returned with the medal she had been working towards for years. When she came home, the celebration took place against a very different backdrop. Her family was still living under a tarpaulin. Their house in Bhogdoiporia Gaon in Assam’s Jorhat district had been washed away in floods the previous month. The family’s fishery had been damaged. Ducks and poultry had been swept away. The buffaloes had to be moved to safer ground. For Janmoni, the gold medal did not mark the end of a struggle. It became part of a family’s attempt to rebuild after losing its home, and a young athlete’s determination to continue chasing a dream that had begun when she was five years old. When the water came On 19 July, floodwaters entered Bhogdoiporia Gaon. An embankment breached around 150 metres from Janmoni’s house, allowing water to rush into the village. The family had to leave their home and move to the embankment. Their losses extended beyond the house. For nearly three years, the family had been raising fish in a fishery. The plan had been to sell the fish and use the money to help fund Janmoni’s trip to Delhi for the National Karate Championship. The flood disrupted that plan too. “The fishery was connected to her competition,” the family explained. It was meant to help pay for her journey. This was not the first time Janmoni’s family had rearranged their lives to keep her in the sport. Earlier, they had sold two buffaloes to meet the expenses of her karate competitions. VIDEO | Delhi: With her home submerged in floodwater and her family forced to take shelter in a relief camp, 17-year-old Janmoni Konwar had every reason to stay back in Assam. Instead, the young karate player from Holmora village in Jorhat district insisted on making the… pic.twitter.com/qDyV0I21M3 — Press Trust of India (@PTI_News) August 8, 2026 For families in remote parts of the country, sporting ambition often comes with costs that have little to do with the training itself. There are journeys to competitions, accommodation, entry fees and equipment. Then there is food. And for an athlete, food is training too. Susanta Das, Janmoni’s coach, points to what he sees as one of the biggest challenges for young athletes in the area. “In these remote places, some families can barely afford three meals a day. So proper nutrition and a specialised diet become difficult,” he tells The Better India . Janmoni does not describe a complicated diet plan. Her food, she says, is home-cooked meals and no cold drinks. But even maintaining that routine becomes difficult when a family has been displaced by a flood. A dream that began at five Janmoni was five when she first began learning karate. There were no air-conditioned training rooms. There were limited facilities. Sometimes, circumstances forced her to train in spaces far removed from what most people would imagine for a national-level athlete. Her coach remembers one quality above all others: consistency. “She is a diligent child,” says Susanta Das. “I always think of how a lotus blooms in the marsh. It is the same with her.” There were times when disasters and disruptions changed where and how she could practise. Sometimes, he says, she trained on the streets. “If I told her to practise for two or three hours, she would do it without stopping. That is her quality,” he says. The results began to show. Janmoni won a bronze medal in 2023. In 2025, she won gold. This year, she was preparing for another national championship when the floods arrived. The journey to Delhi The family had been displaced. The house was gone. Their source of planned income for the championship had been affected. Rail services were also disrupted. For Janmoni and her team, reaching Delhi became a huge challenge to solve. Help arrived after Alakh Pandey, founder of Physics Wallah, learned about Janmoni’s situation during a visit to flood-affected areas of Assam. He supported the team’s travel to Delhi and back, arranged accommodation and provided Rs 3 lakh to Janmoni’s family. Union Minister of State for External Affairs Pabitra Margherita also provided financial assistance of Rs 10,000. With the journey finally possible, Janmoni travelled to Delhi. From a village where floodwater had recently forced her family from their home, she entered the Talkatora Indoor Stadium to compete in the Ashihara category of the National Karate Championship. Janmoni does not describe a complicated diet plan. Her food, she says, is home-cooked meals and no cold drinks. Then came the result she had been waiting for. Gold. The medal represented years of practice, a family’s sacrifices and a journey that, until shortly before the competition, had seemed uncertain. Back to the embankment Janmoni returned to Assam with a national gold medal. Her family, however, was still living under a tarpaulin after their home was washed away. But Janmoni does not speak as though the gold medal is the conclusion of her story. The next journey is already in front of her. Janmoni, on the screen, kept smiling. “ Tu khel India ke liye -You play for India,” her father tells her. The encouragement means a great deal to Janmoni. Her father had once been a footballer himself. Her parents and brother have continued to support her journey, even when doing so has meant making difficult financial decisions. The sale of two buffaloes was one such decision. The fishery was another hope. And now, as the family works to rebuild after the flood, Janmoni is moving into the next stage of her sporting life. ‘They want to be like me’ For all the attention that comes with winning a national gold medal, Janmoni is particularly excited when she speaks about something else. She teaches younger children too. “You know, I also teach little kids,” she says, laughing. Most of her students are girls, though boys train with her as well. “They follow me so much,” she says. “They also love martial arts and are always keen to copy me.” It is perhaps here that Janmoni’s story moves beyond one medal. In a village with limited training facilities, a teenager is now introducing younger children to the same sport. The girls watching her do not just see someone who trains in martial arts. They see someone from their own surroundings who travelled to Delhi and returned with a national gold medal. Now, SAI awaits For a teenager who has trained in difficult circumstances, the opportunity marks a new chapter. It could give her access to structured coaching and help her take the next steps towards competing at higher levels. There is more training to do. More competitions to enter. And younger students back home who are watching. All picture courtesy: Janmoni Konwar

items.title: How 7,000 Residents Built a Zero-Waste Society in Bengaluru | Solved in India
items.blurb: What if an entire apartment society could stop sending almost all its waste to landfills? At Brigade Meadows in Bengaluru, nearly **7,000 residents generate around 800 kg of waste every day**. But instead of sending it all to landfills, the society segregates, composts, recycles and scientifically disposes of its waste. In this episode of **Solved in India**, we explore how Brigade Meadows transformed its waste management system — and what other apartment societies across India can learn from it. Today: 🍃 Around **800 kg of wet waste** is converted into compost 🌾 Compost is supplied to farmers as fertilizer ♻️ Dry and reject waste is sent for recycling and appropriate processing 🏥 Medical waste, diapers and sanitary waste are scientifically disposed of 🥛 Milk packets are cleaned, dried and prepared for recycling 💧 Nearly **6 lakh litres of treated water are recycled every day** for flushing and gardening 📦 Recyclable materials such as cardboard and old electronics also generate funds for the society The result? A community that once struggled with overflowing waste is now diverting almost all of its waste away from landfills. Could this model work in your apartment society? Imagine if more housing societies across India adopted proper wet, dry and reject waste management. How much waste could we keep out of our landfills?
